bookmarks.author: Nadia Kell
bookmarks.title: Permissionless leverage is still unclaimed.
bookmarks.summary: Code and media are the only two forms of leverage that never required permission, and they compound while you sleep. The scarce input is not capital — it is a clear point of view, repeated in public long enough to become trusted.
actions: Pick one narrow claim and repeat it for twelve months
Ship artefacts, not opinions
bookmarks.original:
Capital and labour are permissioned. Code and media are not.

Most people spend a decade asking for permission to use the two forms of leverage that never required it. The asymmetry is absurd, and it is still open.

bookmarks.author: Ivo Marchetti
bookmarks.title: Price is positioning, not arithmetic.
bookmarks.summary: Raising price changes who shows up, what they expect, and how much support they need — usually in your favour. Treating pricing as a spreadsheet output instead of a statement about who the product is for is the actual error.
concepts: Willingness to pay is a segment, not a number
actions: Raise price 30% for new customers only; watch win-rate, not revenue
Name the customer you're deliberately pricing out
bookmarks.original:
You don't have a pricing problem, you have a 'who is this for' problem.

Every time I've doubled price the customers got easier, not harder. The bad-fit buyers were generating 80% of the tickets.

bookmarks.author: Amara Osei
bookmarks.title: Sleep consistency beats sleep duration.
bookmarks.summary: A fixed wake time anchors circadian rhythm more powerfully than total hours in bed, and morning light does more than any supplement on the shelf. Almost every other sleep intervention is downstream of those two.
actions: Fix the wake time and let bedtime drift
Ten minutes of outdoor light before caffeine
bookmarks.original:
The highest-leverage sleep intervention is not a supplement, a mattress, or an app. It is waking up at the same time every day, weekends included, for three weeks.

Everything else is downstream of that.

bookmarks.author: Ben Sørensen
bookmarks.title: Writing in public is a search function.
bookmarks.summary: The point of publishing is not reach but precision: a post read by four hundred of the right people outperforms one read by forty thousand strangers. Write the thing that would make the people you admire email you first.
actions: Write the post only you could have written
Optimise for replies, not impressions
bookmarks.original:
Stop asking how to grow an audience. Ask what you'd need to publish for the five people you most want to work with to email you first.

That post is usually specific, slightly risky, and short.

bookmarks.author: Priya Raghunathan
bookmarks.title: Sort decisions by reversibility before difficulty.
bookmarks.summary: Most bad decisions can be undone, and most people treat them as if they cannot. Filtering choices by whether they are two-way doors removes the majority of deliberation before it starts.
actions: Ask 'can I undo this in a week?' before analysing anything
Spend deliberation budget only on one-way doors
bookmarks.original:
Before you decide whether a decision is right, decide whether it is reversible.

You'll find 90% of what you agonise over is a two-way door you could walk back through this afternoon.

bookmarks.author: Tomas Weiland
bookmarks.title: The cost of interruption is not the interruption.
bookmarks.summary: Attention residue means task-switching degrades the next twenty minutes, not the thirty seconds you spent switching. Batching is not about efficiency — it is about protecting the depth of a single context.
actions: Batch all shallow work into one window
Write the next step down before you switch away
bookmarks.original:
You don't lose 30 seconds when you check Slack mid-task. You lose the next 20 minutes of depth.

The cost of interruption is not the interruption.

bookmarks.author: Helena Vos
bookmarks.title: If you can't describe the role in a sentence, you're hiring a hope.
bookmarks.summary: Vague senior roles fail because the organisation has not yet learned what it needs. Narrow, precisely scoped roles teach you the shape of the job, and they are the only ones you can evaluate honestly at ninety days.
actions: Write the 90-day deliverable before writing the job post
Hire the smallest scope you can define exactly
bookmarks.original:
Every failed senior hire I've made was a role I couldn't describe in one sentence.

If you can't name the first 90 days' output, you're hiring a hope.

bookmarks.author: Marcus Oyelaran
bookmarks.title: Distribution is a product decision made early.
bookmarks.summary: Products that spread have a mechanic inside the core loop that makes sharing rational for the user. Bolting marketing on afterwards means renting attention permanently instead of owning a channel.
actions: Name the share mechanic before building the feature
Ask what makes sharing selfishly rational
bookmarks.original:
'We'll figure out distribution later' is the most expensive sentence in early product work.

Build the channel into the loop, or accept that you'll be renting attention forever.

bookmarks.author: Sana Bakhtiari
bookmarks.title: Ambition without a stopping rule is a treadmill.
bookmarks.summary: Defining what enough looks like in advance is the only mechanism that converts achievement into satisfaction. Without it, each milestone silently resets the baseline and the work never pays out.
actions: Write down the number, the title, the life — then what you do after
Review the stopping rule once a year, in writing
bookmarks.original:
Write down the number, the title, the life. Then write down what you will do when you have it.

If the second list is empty, the first one will never be enough.

bookmarks.author: Elias Fournier
bookmarks.title: Specific knowledge feels like play to you and work to everyone else.
bookmarks.summary: What you cannot be trained for sits at the intersection of genuine curiosity and years of accumulated pattern recognition. You find it by following interest past the point where it still looks like a career move.
actions: Follow the interest that looks least strategic for one month
Notice what you explain to friends unprompted
bookmarks.original:
Specific knowledge is found by following your curiosity past the point where it looks like a career move.

It feels like play to you and work to everyone else. That's the tell.

bookmarks.author: Clara Nyström
bookmarks.title: A note you never revisit is a cost, not an asset.
bookmarks.summary: Capture is the cheap half of thinking; retrieval is the half that pays. A system with no resurfacing mechanism is an archive that quietly bills you attention every time you add to it.
actions: Schedule retrieval, not capture
Delete anything you would not want returned to you
bookmarks.original:
Everyone builds a capture system. Almost nobody builds a retrieval system.

A note you never revisit is not an asset, it's a small recurring tax on your attention.

bookmarks.author: Rina Okafor
bookmarks.title: Nobody remembers your posting streak.
bookmarks.summary: Consistency is overrated as a strategy: one piece of undeniable work outperforms two years of steady output. Volume is the search process you run to find that piece, not the point of the exercise.
actions: Ask which of your last fifty posts was undeniable
Spend a month on one thing instead of thirty on many
bookmarks.original:
Nobody remembers your posting streak. They remember the one thing that was too good to ignore.

Volume is a search process, not a strategy.

briefs.headline: Three of last week's saves are the same idea in different clothes.
briefs.lede: Leverage as repetition, and a March save that disagrees.
paras: Good morning, Sam. You saved eleven posts last week — a light week — and three of them are arguing the same thing: that leverage has less to do with capital than with being willing to repeat one narrow claim in public until people believe it.

I have grouped those three below so you can read them as one argument. Then I pulled forward something you saved in March and never opened, because it makes almost the opposite case, and the disagreement seems more useful than either post alone.
briefs.closer: Nothing else this week needs you today.
briefs.promptQ: You saved a claim about pricing four days ago. What did it say the real problem is, when someone says they have a pricing problem?
briefs.promptA: Not the number — who the product is for. Raising price changes which customers show up and what they expect; the bad-fit buyers were generating most of the support load.

briefs.headline: Nothing new needed you yesterday, so I went looking backwards.
briefs.lede: Two saves about attention, and why your capture system keeps growing.
paras: You saved nothing on Sunday, which is the first quiet day in three weeks. Rather than pad this out, I went back through what you have been saving about attention and found two posts that answer each other.

One argues that the cost of an interruption is the twenty minutes after it, not the interruption. The other argues that a note you never revisit is a recurring tax rather than an asset. Read together they are the same claim about the same resource.
briefs.closer: That is the whole brief. Enjoy the short one.
briefs.promptQ: What did the post on interruptions say you actually lose when you check a message mid-task?
briefs.promptA: The next twenty minutes of depth, not the thirty seconds of switching. Attention residue is the cost, which is why batching protects context rather than time.

briefs.headline: You keep saving arguments about pricing. Here is what they add up to.
briefs.lede: Three saves since March, one consistent claim, one conspicuous gap.
paras: Since March you have saved three posts about pricing and none about discounting or packaging. They agree more than you might expect: price is a statement about who the product is for, and the symptoms people blame on price are usually targeting problems.
The one below about hiring is not about pricing at all, but it is the same error one layer out — vagueness about who, dressed up as a question about how much.
briefs.closer: If you are heading into a pricing decision, the gap in the library is packaging.
briefs.sectionLabel: What your pricing saves agree on
briefs.promptQ: One of your saves names the thing that goes wrong when a role cannot be described in a sentence. What is it?
briefs.promptA: You are hiring a hope. The organisation has not yet learned what it needs, so there is no ninety-day output to evaluate the hire against.

briefs.headline: Two of this week’s saves are decision rules, not ideas.
briefs.lede: Reversibility and stopping rules — both are filters you set once.
paras: Most of what you save is an argument. Two things this week are not: they are rules you could apply this afternoon without agreeing with anyone.
Sort by reversibility before difficulty, and write down what enough looks like before you start. Both work by removing deliberation rather than improving it, which is why I put them together.
briefs.closer: Worth keeping these two somewhere you will see them.
briefs.promptQ: What question does the reversibility post say to ask before analysing any decision?
briefs.promptA: Can I undo this in a week? If yes it is a two-way door and does not deserve the deliberation budget.

briefs.headline: You have saved the same sleep argument three times now.
briefs.lede: Fixed wake time, morning light, everything else downstream.
paras: Three separate posts, three separate months, the same two claims: anchor the wake time, get light early, treat the rest as downstream. I am not going to keep resurfacing this one unless you tell me it is still open.
I have marked the clearest of the three as core so it comes back less often but never disappears.
briefs.closer: A short one. You already know this.
briefs.promptQ: What single intervention does your sleep save call the highest-leverage one?
briefs.promptA: Waking at the same time every day, weekends included, for three weeks. Not a supplement, a mattress, or an app.

briefs.headline: One idea this week was worth the whole week.
briefs.lede: Ambition without a stopping rule, and the streak post that argues with it.
paras: You saved six posts and five of them were variations on advice you already have. The sixth is the one I would keep: ambition without a stated stopping rule never pays out, because each milestone silently resets the baseline.
I paired it with something from March about posting streaks, which is the same argument aimed at output instead of ambition.
briefs.promptQ: What does the stopping-rule post say to write down, and what does it say to write next to it?
briefs.promptA: The number, the title, the life — then what you will do once you have them. If the second list is empty the first will never be enough.

10: How you find it in public

askCorpus.label: Across 3 saves about pricing
paras: Your saves converge on one claim: price is a statement about who the product is for, not an output of a spreadsheet. Two of them go further and argue that the churn and support load you would blame on price is actually a targeting problem wearing a pricing costume.
You have nothing saved about packaging, discounting, or enterprise tiers. If that is where you are heading, the gap is conspicuous — the library will not help you there yet.

askCorpus.label: Across 4 saves about leverage
paras: Your library treats leverage as a distribution problem rather than a capital one. Four ideas, saved eight months apart, land in the same place: pick one narrow claim, repeat it in public, let reputation compound into permission you never had to ask for.

They disagree about volume, which is the interesting part. Rina Okafor argues consistency is overrated and one undeniable piece beats two years of steady output; the others treat volume as the search process that finds that piece.

askCorpus.label: Across 2 saves about sleep
paras: Only two saves, and they agree: fix the wake time, get light early, treat everything else as downstream. Nothing you have saved defends supplements, mattresses, or tracking.
The second one is not about sleep at all — it makes the same shape of argument about attention. You saved them the same week, which is probably why.

askCorpus.label: Across 3 saves about attention
paras: The through-line is that attention has a carrying cost you keep paying after the moment of distraction. An interruption costs the next twenty minutes, not the thirty seconds; a note you never revisit is a small recurring tax rather than an asset.
Both point at the same fix, which you have not saved anything about: scheduling retrieval instead of capture.

askCorpus.label: Across 3 saves about decisions
paras: Two of your saves are rules rather than arguments: sort by reversibility before difficulty, and define what enough looks like before you begin. Both work by removing deliberation rather than improving it.
A third, about hiring, is the same instinct applied to scope — name the ninety-day output before you write the job post.
